title: The Cup of Tea That Left a Radioactive Trail
central_question: How did investigators trace the polonium that killed Alexander Litvinenko, and why has no one stood trial?
content_notes: No trial has taken place. The killers are named only as the findings of a UK public inquiry (2016) and the European Court of Human Rights (2021), always attributed; Lugovoi's denial, Kovtun's denial and his death in 2022, and Russia's denial are stated. Nobody is called a murderer in the narrator's voice. Everyone on screen, Litvinenko included, is an anonymous rim-lit silhouette; no real person's likeness, no flags, emblems or leaders are shown. The illness, the hospital bed and the death are never depicted. The hotel bar, the London streets and the trail map are generic illustrations, not replicas; the map names only verified places. No real document, photograph, logo or court material is imitated. No dialogue is invented. Legal status verified 2026-10-11.

lines.text: Investigators swept a London hotel bar for radiation.
Alexander Litvinenko drank from it: a former Russian security officer and Kremlin critic.
On November 1st, 2006, he had met two Russian men there.
For three weeks, doctors couldn't name the poison.
Only hours before he died did scientists find it: polonium-210.
Its radiation can't even pass through skin, so it's hard to detect.
They traced it across London: a sushi bar, offices, his home.
Traces even turned up at Arsenal's stadium, where the two men watched a match.
Britain charged Andrei Lugovoi with murder. Russia refused to extradite him.
In 2016, a UK public inquiry concluded Lugovoi and Dmitry Kovtun poisoned him.
It found they had tried once before, in October.
It said the operation was probably approved by President Putin and FSB chief Patrushev.
Lugovoi has always denied it. So did Kovtun, who died in 2022.
In 2021, the European Court of Human Rights held Russia responsible.
Next month marks 20 years. No one has ever stood trial.
Which case should we crack next? Tell us in the comments.

claims.text: After Litvinenko's death, investigators surveyed the Millennium Hotel's Pine Bar for polonium-210 contamination; the contamination map ran from lower readings across the bar to the highest at the table where the group sat.

The highest readings in the bar came from the teapot Litvinenko drank from (the largest reading from its spout), as described in reporting on the 2016 inquiry; the inquiry released images of the teapot.
At the Pine Bar meeting on 1 November 2006 Litvinenko drank green tea from the pot; the two other men had gin.
Alexander Litvinenko was a former officer of Russia's FSB security service who came to Britain in 2000, became a prominent Kremlin critic, and lived in London.
On 1 November 2006 Litvinenko met Andrei Lugovoi and Dmitry Kovtun at the Pine Bar of the Millennium Hotel, Grosvenor Square, London.
Litvinenko fell ill on 1 November 2006 and was taken to hospital.
For about three weeks the cause of his illness was not identified: the early clinical picture resembled infection or chemical poisoning such as thallium.

Polonium-210 was identified only hours before he died (NBC: about two hours; EUvsDisinfo: six hours after the urine result); the Health Protection Agency announced it on 24 November. Polonium-210 is described as a rare, radioactive element.
Litvinenko died in London on 23 November 2006.

FUN FACT: polonium-210 emits alpha radiation, which is stopped by a thin layer of matter such as skin; ordinary Geiger counters pick up beta and gamma radiation, and alpha radiation needs special detectors (Aldermaston identified it by its 5.3 MeV alpha signature).

Investigators traced polonium contamination to sites across London, including the Itsu sushi restaurant near Piccadilly, an office block and a Mayfair address, and Litvinenko's north London home; by 30 November traces had been found at 12 sites, and dozens of scenes were assessed.

Two British Airways Boeing 767s at Heathrow showed traces of radioactive material at very low levels (late November 2006); officials did not then say whether it was polonium-210, and the health risk was called low.

FUN FACT: traces of polonium-210 were found at Arsenal's Emirates Stadium, where Lugovoi and Kovtun watched Arsenal v CSKA Moscow on the evening of 1 November 2006; the Health Protection Agency called the levels barely detectable and no risk to the public.
In May 2007 the Director of Public Prosecutions said there was sufficient evidence to charge Andrei Lugovoi with Litvinenko's murder, and Britain requested his extradition.
On 5 July 2007 Russia formally refused to extradite Lugovoi, citing article 61 of its constitution (a Russian citizen cannot be handed over to another state).

The UK public inquiry chaired by Sir Robert Owen reported on 21 January 2016 that Lugovoi and Kovtun deliberately poisoned Litvinenko with polonium-210 at the Pine Bar on 1 November 2006 (placing it in the teapot), probably under the direction of the FSB. This is an inquiry finding, not a criminal verdict; neither man has been tried.
The inquiry found that the two men had made an earlier attempt to poison Litvinenko with polonium-210 at a meeting at the Erinys office on 16 October 2006.
The inquiry concluded that the FSB operation to kill Litvinenko was 'probably approved' by Nikolai Patrushev, then director of the FSB, and also by President Putin.
Lugovoi has denied any involvement since 2007, calling the accusations politically motivated, and disputed the 2016 findings; Kovtun also denied it (in 2015 he suggested the death was an accident).
Dmitry Kovtun died in Moscow in June 2022 (reported as COVID-19, citing TASS).
Russia rejected the inquiry's findings and denies involvement; its ambassador called the inquiry a 'blatant provocation'.

On 21 September 2021 the European Court of Human Rights (Carter v Russia) held Russia responsible for Litvinenko's killing, finding a strong prima facie case that Lugovoi and Kovtun acted as agents of the Russian state.
Litvinenko died on 23 November 2006: November 2026 marks 20 years (this episode is published in October 2026).

No one has been tried for Litvinenko's death: Russia refused extradition, Kovtun died in 2022, and no trial or new legal step was found on 2026-10-11 (Lugovoi remains under UK sanctions, notice amended March 2025).
